title: Perineal trauma: recognising and categorising
summary: Classifying perineal tears and knowing when a repair needs an appropriately trained clinician.
redFlags: Any suspected third- or fourth-degree tear (obstetric anal sphincter injury, OASI) must be repaired in theatre by an appropriately trained/experienced clinician — do not attempt this repair outside that setting.

blocks.heading: Classifying the trauma
bullets: First degree: injury to perineal skin and/or vaginal mucosa only.
Second degree: injury to perineal muscles but not the anal sphincter.

Third degree: injury involving the anal sphincter complex — subdivided by how much of the external sphincter is torn; VERIFY the exact subdivision definitions (commonly described as 3a/3b/3c) against current local training.
Fourth degree: injury involving the anal sphincter complex and the anal epithelium.

blocks.heading: Risk factors for obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASI)
bullets: First vaginal birth, instrumental birth, a larger baby, a prolonged second stage, and a persistent occipito-posterior position are commonly cited risk factors.
VERIFY the full current risk-factor list against RCOG guidance, as it is periodically updated.

blocks.heading: Repair
bullets: First- and second-degree tears can be repaired per local competency and training.
Third- and fourth-degree tears (OASI) require repair in theatre, usually by an obstetrician with appropriate training — do not attempt this repair outside that setting.
Antibiotics and laxatives are commonly given after OASI repair — VERIFY exact local protocol and dosing.

blocks.heading: What to document
bullets: Clear description (or diagram) of the trauma and its classification.
Repair performed, by whom, and materials used.
Postnatal advice given — pelvic floor exercises, follow-up clinic referral for third/fourth-degree tears.

citations.section: GTG 29 — The Management of Third- and Fourth-Degree Perineal Tears (OASI)
